S01.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S01.1.t0.eleven_v3
S01.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: In October, 2023, the average 30 -year fixed mortgage rate in the U .S. hit its highest level since 2000.

S02.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S02.2.t0.eleven_v3
S02.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: Now a letter from her lender offers a lower rate with a bill at the bottom.

S02.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S02.3.t0.eleven_v3
S02.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: How far must her rate fall before that bill pays itself back?

S04.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S04.1.t0.eleven_v3
S04.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: This is one decision followed through three households.

S04.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S04.2.t0.eleven_v3
S04.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: By the end, you will see the rate drop that pays that bill back within three years for three different loan sizes.

S04.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S04.3.t0.eleven_v3
S04.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: The answer starts with how rates got here.

S05.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S05.1.t0.eleven_v3
S05.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: One week in January 2021, the average 30 -year fixed rate was 2 .65%, the lowest in the weekly record.

S05.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S05.2.t0.eleven_v3
S05.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: From there, it climbed to the peak you saw at the start.

S05.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S05.3.t0.eleven_v3
S05.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: That line is history, not a forecast, and it covers the U .S. only.

S06.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S06.2.t0.eleven_v3
S06.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: three in 10 30 year home purchase loans made in 2023 carried a rate of 7 % or more.

S06.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S06.3.t0.eleven_v3
S06.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: Nora lives in one of those three houses.

S07.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S07.1.t0.eleven_v3
S07.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: She moved for a new job in October 2023 and bought her first home.

S07.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S07.2.t0.eleven_v3
S07.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: She knew the rate was high. The move could not wait.

S07.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S07.4.t0.eleven_v3
S07.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: All dollar amounts here are nominal.

S07.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S07.5.t0.eleven_v3
S07.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: Her rate, 7 .62%, was the average that month.

S08.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S08.1.t0.eleven_v3
S08.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: Almost three years later, her lender has a proposal.

S08.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S08.2.t0.eleven_v3
S08.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: It is a refinance, a new loan that pays off the old one.

S08.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S08.3.t0.eleven_v3
S08.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: The offer is priced at the latest weekly average, 7 .03%.

S09.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S09.1.t0.eleven_v3
S09.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: That is just over half a percentage point below her rate.

S09.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S09.2.t0.eleven_v3
S09.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: Her monthly payment would fall by $221.

S09.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S09.4.t0.eleven_v3
S09.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: That drop is in the rate itself, not the fees that lenders call points.

S09.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S09.5.t0.eleven_v3
S09.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: Then there is the line at the bottom of the letter.

S10.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S10.1.t0.eleven_v3
S10.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: $5 ,124 in loan costs, paid in cash at closing.

S10.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S10.2.t0.eleven_v3
S10.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: That covers the fees for making the loan plus any points she pays to lower the rate.

S10.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S10.3.t0.eleven_v3
S10.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: If a letter like this has reached you, this is the math behind it.

S10.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S10.4.t0.eleven_v3
S10.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: Nora is an illustrative borrower, but her loan and that bill are the real medians from nearly half a million refinances in 2025.

S11.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S11.1.t0.eleven_v3
S11.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: So is a bill like this worth paying?

S11.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S11.2.t0.eleven_v3
S11.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: Nora hears two answers, and they do not agree.

S12.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S12.1.t0.eleven_v3
S12.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: You may have heard that a refinance only pays off once rates fall a full percentage point.

S12.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S12.2.t0.eleven_v3
S12.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: We tested that one point line.

S12.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S12.3.t0.eleven_v3
S12.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: her offer falls short of it.

S12.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S12.4.t0.eleven_v3
S12.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: Simple Division says otherwise, $5 ,124 divided by 221 is about 24 months.

S12.6.t0.eleven_v3.name: S12.6.t0.eleven_v3
S12.6.t0.eleven_v3.text: two years, and the bill is paid back.

S13.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S13.2.t0.eleven_v3
S13.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: neither one, as it turns out.

S13.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S13.3.t0.eleven_v3
S13.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: The one -point line never looks at the bill.

S14.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S14.2.t0.eleven_v3
S14.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: Break Even is the month when what Nora has saved covers the bill.

S14.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S14.3.t0.eleven_v3
S14.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: Every month, her payment is $221 smaller.

S14.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S14.4.t0.eleven_v3
S14.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: Stack those months up and sooner or later they reach the bill.

S14.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S14.5.t0.eleven_v3
S14.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: But while the savings stack up, something else is happening to what she owes.

S15.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S15.1.t0.eleven_v3
S15.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: She has made 35 payments on her old loan.

S15.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S15.2.t0.eleven_v3
S15.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: A new loan starts the 30 -year clock over.

S15.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S15.3.t0.eleven_v3
S15.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: It is like two staircases down to zero, and the new one has shallower steps at the top.

S15.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S15.4.t0.eleven_v3
S15.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: In the early years of any mortgage, more of each payment goes to interest and less goes to paying down the loan.

S15.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S15.5.t0.eleven_v3
S15.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: So after a refinance, she pays down what she owes more slowly than she would have.

S15.6.t0.eleven_v3.name: S15.6.t0.eleven_v3
S15.6.t0.eleven_v3.text: By month 24, that difference has a price.

S16.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S16.1.t0.eleven_v3
S16.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: At month 24, she owes $1 ,133 more than she would have on the old loan.

S16.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S16.3.t0.eleven_v3
S16.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: No letter mentions it and the Division never sees it.

S16.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S16.4.t0.eleven_v3
S16.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: It is a real cost, even though it never arrives as a bill.

S16.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S16.5.t0.eleven_v3
S16.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: Count that gap and the clock keeps running.

S17.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S17.1.t0.eleven_v3
S17.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: With the gap counted, the bill comes back at month 30.

S17.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S17.4.t0.eleven_v3
S17.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: It still comes back just later than the division promised.

S17.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S17.5.t0.eleven_v3
S17.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: And the smaller the drop, the more that gap matters.

S18.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S18.1.t0.eleven_v3
S18.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: Suppose the offer had cut her rate by only a quarter of a percentage point.

S18.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S18.4.t0.eleven_v3
S18.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: longer, but still a finish line.

S19.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S19.1.t0.eleven_v3
S19.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: Counting what she owes, the bill does not come back before her old loan would have been paid off.

S19.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S19.3.t0.eleven_v3
S19.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: So what about a full point?

S20.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S20.1.t0.eleven_v3
S20.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: At a full percentage point, her bill comes back in 18 months.

S20.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S20.3.t0.eleven_v3
S20.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: that is well inside three years.

S20.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S20.4.t0.eleven_v3
S20.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: Somewhere between a quarter point and a full point is her line.

S21.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S21.1.t0.eleven_v3
S21.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: At half a point, the bill comes back in exactly 36 months.

S21.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S21.2.t0.eleven_v3
S21.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: So to pay it back within three years, Nora needs a drop of half a point.

S21.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S21.3.t0.eleven_v3
S21.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: Her real offer, just over half a point, pays back at month 30.

S21.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S21.5.t0.eleven_v3
S21.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: that is half of the one -point line, and the offer on her table clears it.

S21.6.t0.eleven_v3.name: S21.6.t0.eleven_v3
S21.6.t0.eleven_v3.text: but is half a point the line for everyone?

S22.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S22.1.t0.eleven_v3
S22.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: Welt borrowed the same month as Nora for a smaller house.

S22.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S22.2.t0.eleven_v3
S22.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: He teaches at the high school across town and the house was what he could afford on one salary.

S22.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S22.4.t0.eleven_v3
S22.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: His letter offers the same drop and he reads it the same way, down to the last line.

S22.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S22.5.t0.eleven_v3
S22.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: The bill at the bottom is $3 ,667.

S22.7.t0.eleven_v3.name: S22.7.t0.eleven_v3
S22.7.t0.eleven_v3.text: Why did the bill barely shrink when the loan did?

S23.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S23.1.t0.eleven_v3
S23.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: In the 2025 data, the bill grows far more slowly than the loan.

S23.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S23.2.t0.eleven_v3
S23.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: For Walt, it comes to about 3 .2 % of his loan.

S23.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S23.3.t0.eleven_v3
S23.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: For Nora, the same kind of bill is a much smaller slice of what she borrowed.

S24.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S24.1.t0.eleven_v3
S24.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: The same drop saves Walt just $68 a month.

S24.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S24.2.t0.eleven_v3
S24.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: With the balance cap counted, his bill comes back in month 75.

S24.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S24.4.t0.eleven_v3
S24.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: That is a long time to wait for a letter to pay off.

S24.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S24.5.t0.eleven_v3
S24.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: and if he sells before the clock gets there.

S25.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S25.1.t0.eleven_v3
S25.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: If Walt sells after three years, the refinance leaves him $1 ,777 behind.

S25.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S25.3.t0.eleven_v3
S25.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: He paid the bill upfront, and by then the savings had not caught up.

S25.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S25.4.t0.eleven_v3
S25.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: For him, the refinance would have been a cost, not a saving.

S25.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S25.5.t0.eleven_v3
S25.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: To pay his bill back within three years, how far would his rate have to fall?

S26.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S26.1.t0.eleven_v3
S26.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: by a little more than one full percentage point, 1 .12.

S26.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S26.3.t0.eleven_v3
S26.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: That is more than the one -point line.

S26.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S26.4.t0.eleven_v3
S26.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: For a loan this small, even the full point line falls short.

S26.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S26.5.t0.eleven_v3
S26.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: At the other end, the opposite happens.

S27.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S27.1.t0.eleven_v3
S27.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: Angeli borrowed that same month, too.

S27.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S27.2.t0.eleven_v3
S27.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: She and her husband bought a larger place for a growing family.

S27.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S27.3.t0.eleven_v3
S27.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: Her loan was $655 ,000, still under the conforming limit.

S27.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S27.4.t0.eleven_v3
S27.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: She got the same drop and a bill of $5 ,514, close to what Nora pays.

S27.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S27.5.t0.eleven_v3
S27.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: almost the same bill spread over a much bigger loan.

S27.6.t0.eleven_v3.name: S27.6.t0.eleven_v3
S27.6.t0.eleven_v3.text: Her monthly savings are far bigger than what Nora saves.

S28.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S28.1.t0.eleven_v3
S28.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: If she sold after three years, she would come out $5 ,250 a head.

S28.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S28.3.t0.eleven_v3
S28.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: To pay her bill back within three years, she needs a drop of only about a third of a point.

S28.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S28.5.t0.eleven_v3
S28.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: So back to the question Nora started with.

S29.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S29.1.t0.eleven_v3
S29.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: How far must her rate fall before that bill pays itself back?

S29.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S29.2.t0.eleven_v3
S29.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: To pay the bill back within three years, the drop depends on the loan.

S29.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S29.3.t0.eleven_v3
S29.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: about a third of a point for Angeli.

S29.6.t0.eleven_v3.name: S29.6.t0.eleven_v3
S29.6.t0.eleven_v3.text: The one -point line fits none of them.

S29.7.t0.eleven_v3.name: S29.7.t0.eleven_v3
S29.7.t0.eleven_v3.text: Half a point is the line for Nora, not for everyone.

S29.9.t0.eleven_v3.name: S29.9.t0.eleven_v3
S29.9.t0.eleven_v3.text: These are average rates, median bills, and three illustrative households. So a real rate, a real bill, and a real balance will differ.

S29.10.t0.eleven_v3.name: S29.10.t0.eleven_v3
S29.10.t0.eleven_v3.text: which leaves one number that only you know.

S30.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S30.1.t0.eleven_v3
S30.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: How long will you stay in the house?

S30.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S30.2.t0.eleven_v3
S30.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: Nobody else can answer that, and the answer changes the math.

S30.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S30.3.t0.eleven_v3
S30.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: If Nora sells after three years, she comes out $1 ,039 a head.

S31.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S31.1.t0.eleven_v3
S31.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: If she stays seven years, she comes out $8 ,093 a head.

S31.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S31.3.t0.eleven_v3
S31.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: Seven years is not a prediction.

S31.4.t0.eleven_v3.name: S31.4.t0.eleven_v3
S31.4.t0.eleven_v3.text: It is one of the two horizons we tested and the longer she stays, the further the savings run past the bill.

S31.5.t0.eleven_v3.name: S31.5.t0.eleven_v3
S31.5.t0.eleven_v3.text: How long do you picture yourself there?

S32.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S32.1.t0.eleven_v3
S32.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: Here is how we built these numbers.

S32.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S32.2.t0.eleven_v3
S32.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: Rates come from Freddie Mac through the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

S32.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S32.3.t0.eleven_v3
S32.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: Loans and loan costs come from federal mortgage records for 2025.

S32.7.t0.eleven_v3.name: S32.7.t0.eleven_v3
S32.7.t0.eleven_v3.text: The full method and the data are linked in the description.

S34.1.t0.eleven_v3.name: S34.1.t0.eleven_v3
S34.1.t0.eleven_v3.text: Nora started with one letter and one question.

S34.2.t0.eleven_v3.name: S34.2.t0.eleven_v3
S34.2.t0.eleven_v3.text: The answer turned out to depend on three things she already knew, her loan, her bill, and how long she plans to stay.

S34.3.t0.eleven_v3.name: S34.3.t0.eleven_v3
S34.3.t0.eleven_v3.text: If there is a money decision you would like to see tested this way, the comments are open.

S01.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: In October, 2023, the average 30 year fixed mortgage rate in the US hit its highest level since 2000.

S02.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: Now a letter from her lender offers a lower rate with a bill at the bottom.

S04.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: By the end, you will see the rate drop that pays that bill back within three years for three different loan sizes.

S06.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: Nora lives in one of those three houses.

S08.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: Almost three years later, her lender has a proposal.

S08.2.t1.eleven_v3.name: S08.2.t1.eleven_v3
S08.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: It is a refinance, a new loan that pays off the old one.

S08.3.t1.eleven_v3.name: S08.3.t1.eleven_v3
S08.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: The offer is priced at the latest weekly average, 7 .03%.

S09.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S09.1.t1.eleven_v3
S09.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: that is just over half a percentage point below her rate.

S09.2.t1.eleven_v3.name: S09.2.t1.eleven_v3
S09.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: Her monthly payment would fall by $221.

S09.4.t1.eleven_v3.name: S09.4.t1.eleven_v3
S09.4.t1.eleven_v3.text: That drop is in the rate itself, not the fees that lenders call points.

S09.5.t1.eleven_v3.name: S09.5.t1.eleven_v3
S09.5.t1.eleven_v3.text: Then there is the line at the bottom of the letter.

S10.2.t1.eleven_v3.name: S10.2.t1.eleven_v3
S10.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: That covers the fees for making the loan, plus any points she pays to lower the rate.

S10.3.t1.eleven_v3.name: S10.3.t1.eleven_v3
S10.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: If a letter like this has reached you, this is the math behind it.

S10.4.t1.eleven_v3.name: S10.4.t1.eleven_v3
S10.4.t1.eleven_v3.text: Nora is an illustrative borrower, but her loan and that bill are the real medians from nearly half a million refinances in 2025.

S11.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S11.1.t1.eleven_v3
S11.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: So is a bill like this worth paying?

S11.2.t1.eleven_v3.name: S11.2.t1.eleven_v3
S11.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: Nora hears two answers, and they do not agree.

S12.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S12.1.t1.eleven_v3
S12.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: You may have heard that a refinance only pays off once rates fall a full percentage point.

S12.2.t1.eleven_v3.name: S12.2.t1.eleven_v3
S12.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: We tested that one point line.

S12.3.t1.eleven_v3.name: S12.3.t1.eleven_v3
S12.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: her offer falls short of it.

S12.4.t1.eleven_v3.name: S12.4.t1.eleven_v3
S12.4.t1.eleven_v3.text: Simple division says otherwise, $5 ,124 divided by 221 is about 24 months.

S12.6.t1.eleven_v3.name: S12.6.t1.eleven_v3
S12.6.t1.eleven_v3.text: Two years and the bill is paid back.

S13.2.t1.eleven_v3.name: S13.2.t1.eleven_v3
S13.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: neither one, as it turns out.

S13.3.t1.eleven_v3.name: S13.3.t1.eleven_v3
S13.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: The one -point line never looks at the bill.

S14.2.t1.eleven_v3.name: S14.2.t1.eleven_v3
S14.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: Break Even is the month when what Nora has saved covers the bill.

S14.4.t1.eleven_v3.name: S14.4.t1.eleven_v3
S14.4.t1.eleven_v3.text: Stack those months up, and sooner or later, they reach the bill.

S14.5.t1.eleven_v3.name: S14.5.t1.eleven_v3
S14.5.t1.eleven_v3.text: But while the savings stack up, something else is happening to what she owes.

S15.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S15.1.t1.eleven_v3
S15.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: She has made 35 payments on her old loan.

S15.2.t1.eleven_v3.name: S15.2.t1.eleven_v3
S15.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: A new loan starts the 30 -year clock over.

S15.3.t1.eleven_v3.name: S15.3.t1.eleven_v3
S15.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: It is like two staircases down to zero, and the new one has shallower steps at the top.

S15.4.t1.eleven_v3.name: S15.4.t1.eleven_v3
S15.4.t1.eleven_v3.text: In the early years of any mortgage, more of each payment goes to interest and less goes to paying down the loan.

S15.5.t1.eleven_v3.name: S15.5.t1.eleven_v3
S15.5.t1.eleven_v3.text: So, after a refinance, she pays down what she owes more slowly than she would have.

S16.3.t1.eleven_v3.name: S16.3.t1.eleven_v3
S16.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: No letter mentions it, and the Division never sees it.

S16.4.t1.eleven_v3.name: S16.4.t1.eleven_v3
S16.4.t1.eleven_v3.text: It is a real cost, even though it never arrives as a bill.

S16.5.t1.eleven_v3.name: S16.5.t1.eleven_v3
S16.5.t1.eleven_v3.text: Count that gap and the clock keeps running.

S17.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S17.1.t1.eleven_v3
S17.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: With the gap counted, the bill comes back at month 30.

S17.4.t1.eleven_v3.name: S17.4.t1.eleven_v3
S17.4.t1.eleven_v3.text: It still comes back just later than the division promised.

S17.5.t1.eleven_v3.name: S17.5.t1.eleven_v3
S17.5.t1.eleven_v3.text: And the smaller the drop, the more that gap matters.

S18.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S18.1.t1.eleven_v3
S18.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: Suppose the offer had cut her rate by only a quarter of a percentage point.

S18.4.t1.eleven_v3.name: S18.4.t1.eleven_v3
S18.4.t1.eleven_v3.text: longer, but still a finish line.

S19.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S19.1.t1.eleven_v3
S19.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: Counting what she owes, the bill does not come back before her old loan would have been paid off.

S19.3.t1.eleven_v3.name: S19.3.t1.eleven_v3
S19.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: So what about a full point?

S20.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S20.1.t1.eleven_v3
S20.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: At a full percentage point, her bill comes back in 18 months.

S20.3.t1.eleven_v3.name: S20.3.t1.eleven_v3
S20.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: That is well inside three years.

S20.4.t1.eleven_v3.name: S20.4.t1.eleven_v3
S20.4.t1.eleven_v3.text: Somewhere between a quarter point and a full point is her line.

S21.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S21.1.t1.eleven_v3
S21.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: At half a point, the bill comes back in exactly 36 months.

S21.2.t1.eleven_v3.name: S21.2.t1.eleven_v3
S21.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: So to pay it back within three years, Nora needs a drop of half a point.

S21.3.t1.eleven_v3.name: S21.3.t1.eleven_v3
S21.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: her real offer, just over half a point, pays back at month 30.

S21.5.t1.eleven_v3.name: S21.5.t1.eleven_v3
S21.5.t1.eleven_v3.text: That is half of the one point line and the offer on her table clears it.

S21.6.t1.eleven_v3.name: S21.6.t1.eleven_v3
S21.6.t1.eleven_v3.text: but is half a point the line for everyone?

S22.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S22.1.t1.eleven_v3
S22.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: Walt borrowed the same month as Nora for a smaller house.

S22.2.t1.eleven_v3.name: S22.2.t1.eleven_v3

S22.7.t1.eleven_v3.text: Why did the bill barely shrink when the loan did?

S23.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: In the 2025 data, the bill grows far more slowly than the loan.

S23.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: For Walt, it comes to about 3 .2 % of his loan.

S23.3.t1.eleven_v3.text: For Nora, the same kind of bill is a much smaller slice of what she borrowed.

S24.1.t1.eleven_v3.name: S24.1.t1.eleven_v3
S24.1.t1.eleven_v3.text: The same drop saves Walt just $68 a month.

S24.2.t1.eleven_v3.text: With a balance gap counted, his bill comes back in month 75.

S24.4.t1.eleven_v3.name: S24.4.t1.eleven_v3
S24.4.t1.eleven_v3.text: That is a long time to wait for a letter to pay off.
